## 1. Purpose

This module prepares the real *Coffea arabica* genomic data used throughout the
prediction workflow. The population contains 195 individuals derived from
crosses involving the Catuaí group and Timor Hybrid germplasm. Genotyping was
performed by Capture-Seq, producing the SNP panel used as the genomic input.

The module has four goals:

- describe the genomic and phenotypic inputs used for prediction;
- align the 195 genomic profiles with their corresponding individual BLUPs;
- apply the same marker quality-control criteria to every prediction method;
- save one common object for validation, GBLUP-A, GBLUP-AD, GBLUP-ADE,
  regularized ANN, and model comparison.

No genomic prediction model is fitted here. All downstream methods receive the
same individuals, phenotypic targets, and retained marker panel.

The steps are presented in their analytical order: inspect the input data,
match plants across genotype and phenotype records, describe the population and
trait targets, examine SNP coding, apply marker quality control, and assemble the
shared object used by pre-validation and genomic prediction. R01 provides the
plant-level BLUPs, while R03 consumes the prepared object created here.

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  echo = TRUE,
  warning = FALSE,
  message = FALSE,
  cache = FALSE,
  fig.align = "center",
  out.width = "100%"
)

options(stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
```

## 2. Software packages and quality-control settings

The genomic analyses use three packages:

- **`knitr`** formats data summaries as HTML tables;
- **`ggplot2`** constructs the marker-quality figure;
- **`ggthemes`** provides `theme_gdocs()` and matching color scales.

```{r packages, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
library(knitr)
library(ggplot2)
library(ggthemes)
```

The marker-quality criteria are fixed before preprocessing:

```{r quality-control-settings}
CALL_RATE_MIN <- 0.90
MAF_MIN <- 0.05
```

## 3. Genomic and phenotypic inputs

The genomic input contains individuals in rows and SNPs in columns. The
phenotypic input contains the individual BLUPs estimated first by the
phenotypic mixed model for cercosporiosis (`Cer`), leaf-miner incidence (`BM`),
and the production-related trait (`LP`). These BLUPs are aligned with
individual genotype identifiers before cross-validation partitions are generated.

### 3.1 Reading the input files and dimensions

The Capture-Seq genotypes are read from `geno_real.rds` and retained in
`G_raw` with their original individual row labels and SNP column order.
The `real_phenotype_blups.rds` object comes from R01 and contains the
three adjusted phenotypic targets for each experimental plant. The input
table compares their dimensions before any individual matching or marker
filtering.

```{r read-inputs}
geno_raw <- readRDS(
  "data/dados_reais/geno_real.rds"
)

blups <- readRDS(
  "output/real/phenotype/real_phenotype_blups.rds"
)

G_raw <- as.matrix(geno_raw)

input_summary <- data.frame(
  Input = c(
    "Capture-Seq genotype panel",
    "Individual BLUPs"
  ),
  Individuals = c(
    nrow(G_raw),
    nrow(blups)
  ),
  Variables = c(
    ncol(G_raw),
    3L
  ),
  Description = c(
    "Raw SNP markers",
    "Cer, BM, and LP"
  ),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

input_summary |>
  knitr::kable(
    format = "html",
    row.names = FALSE,
    table.attr = 'class="table table-striped table-hover table-bordered" width="100%"',
    caption = "Real-data inputs used in the genomic-prediction workflow",
    col.names = c("Input", "Individuals", "Variables", "Description")
  )
```

Capture-Seq produced `r format(ncol(G_raw), big.mark = ",")` SNPs for the
`r nrow(G_raw)` genotyped individuals. The phenotype module supplies one BLUP
for each of these individuals and each of the three prediction traits.

### 3.2 Inspecting genomic and phenotypic records

The genomic matrix contains one row per genotyped plant and one column per SNP.
The example below shows the first six genomic row labels and four SNP columns;
the full `G_raw` matrix remains unchanged. The genotype values are represented
by the original `-1/0/1` coding, which is explained in Section 6.

```{r genomic-input-example}
genotype_example <- data.frame(
  Genotype_ID = rownames(G_raw)[1:6],
  G_raw[1:6, 1:4, drop = FALSE],
  check.names = FALSE
)

genotype_example |>
  knitr::kable(
    format = "html",
    row.names = FALSE,
    table.attr = 'class="table table-striped table-hover table-bordered" width="100%"',
    caption = "Example of six raw Capture-Seq profiles at four SNP loci"
  )
```

The phenotypic file has one row per target plant, rather than one row per
plant-year observation. The `Phenotype_ID` identifies the saved BLUP record,
`ID_Planta` is its permanent field identifier, and `Progenie`, `Planta`,
and `Populacao` retain the experimental identity. The three final columns
contain the previously estimated `Cer`, `BM`, and `LP` BLUPs.

```{r phenotype-input-example}
head(
  blups[, c("Phenotype_ID", "ID_Planta", "Progenie", "Planta",
            "Populacao", "Cer", "BM", "LP"), drop = FALSE],
  6L
) |>
  knitr::kable(
    format = "html",
    row.names = FALSE,
    table.attr = 'class="table table-striped table-hover table-bordered" width="100%"',
    digits = 4,
    caption = "Example of six individual phenotypic BLUP records from R01"
  )
```

These two samples display the source structures without changing the records.
The following section establishes which genomic and phenotypic labels refer to
the same individual before constructing the common genomic matrix.

## 4. Individual identification and alignment

### 4.1 Matching individual identifiers

The genomic rows use labels of the form `PROG 1_1`, where the first number
identifies the progeny and the second identifies the plant within that progeny.
The phenotype object stores these two components separately as `Progenie` and
`Planta`. For example, the R01 record `PROG01_PL01` (`Progenie = 1`,
`Planta = 1`) corresponds to the genomic row `PROG 1_1`.

The `Genotype_ID` is constructed from `Progenie` and `Planta`, while the
permanent field identifier `ID_Planta` is preserved separately.
`match()` locates each constructed label among the genomic row names.
The alignment summary reports the numbers of identifiers on both sides,
unmatched records, and successful matches. The existing checks require a
unique one-to-one correspondence before `G_raw` is reordered with
`genotype_match`. Its SNP column order and genotype values are preserved.

```{r individual-alignment}
blups$Genotype_ID <- paste0(
  "PROG ",
  blups$Progenie,
  "_",
  blups$Planta
)

genotype_match <- match(
  blups$Genotype_ID,
  rownames(G_raw)
)

alignment_summary <- data.frame(
  Check = c(
    "Phenotypic individuals",
    "Genotypic individuals",
    "Unique phenotypic genomic IDs",
    "Unique genomic row IDs",
    "Phenotypes without genotype",
    "Genotypes without phenotype",
    "One-to-one matches"
  ),
  Value = c(
    nrow(blups),
    nrow(G_raw),
    length(unique(blups$Genotype_ID)),
    length(unique(rownames(G_raw))),
    sum(!blups$Genotype_ID %in% rownames(G_raw)),
    sum(!rownames(G_raw) %in% blups$Genotype_ID),
    sum(!is.na(genotype_match))
  ),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

alignment_summary |>
  knitr::kable(
    format = "html",
    row.names = FALSE,
    table.attr = 'class="table table-striped table-hover table-bordered" width="100%"',
    caption = "Individual alignment between phenotype and genotype data",
    col.names = c("Check", "Value")
  )

stopifnot(
  nrow(blups) == 195L,
  nrow(G_raw) == 195L,
  length(unique(blups$Genotype_ID)) == 195L,
  length(unique(rownames(G_raw))) == 195L,
  !anyNA(genotype_match),
  length(unique(genotype_match)) == 195L,
  setequal(blups$Genotype_ID, rownames(G_raw))
)

G <- G_raw[
  genotype_match,
  ,
  drop = FALSE
]

stopifnot(
  identical(
    rownames(G),
    blups$Genotype_ID
  )
)

individuals <- data.frame(
  Phenotype_ID = blups$Phenotype_ID,
  Genotype_ID = blups$Genotype_ID,
  ID_Planta = blups$ID_Planta,
  Progenie = blups$Progenie,
  Planta = blups$Planta,
  Populacao = blups$Populacao,
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

rownames(G) <- individuals$Phenotype_ID
```

The common genomic matrix is now ordered exactly as the phenotype table. The
stable `Phenotype_ID` is used as the row name passed to all downstream modules.

### 4.2 Inspecting the aligned individuals

The `individuals` table retains both forms of the identifier alongside
the original experimental fields. The example below shows the first six
correspondences after matching, including the distinction between the
phenotypic label, genomic label, and permanent plant identifier.

```{r aligned-individual-example}
head(individuals, 6L) |>
  knitr::kable(
    format = "html",
    row.names = FALSE,
    table.attr = 'class="table table-striped table-hover table-bordered" width="100%"',
    caption = "First six phenotype-to-genotype matches",
    col.names = c(
      "Phenotype ID", "Genotype ID", "Plant ID",
      "Progeny", "Plant", "Population"
    )
  )
```

The alignment does not estimate new BLUPs or filter SNPs. It places the 195
genomic profiles in the same order as the saved phenotype targets and labels
the rows of `G` using `Phenotype_ID`. Sections 5–8 then describe this
aligned population and prepare its marker panel.

## 5. Population and trait structure

### 5.1 Progeny membership and population size

The aligned population contains 195 individual plants from 13 experimental
progenies, with 15 plants in each progeny. Progeny membership comes from the
`Progenie` field retained from R01, not from the SNP values. Each plant is
counted once, even though its original phenotypic observations span three
evaluation years.

\[
13\ \text{progenies}\times15\ \text{plants}=195\ \text{individuals}.
\]

The following code constructs the `family` labels and counts the individuals
in each progeny. It displays the progenies in numeric order for readability
without changing the `family_table` object passed to the saved summaries.

```{r population-structure}
family <- paste0(
  "PROG ",
  individuals$Progenie
)

family_size <- sort(
  table(family)
)

family_table <- data.frame(
  Progeny = names(family_size),
  Individuals = as.integer(family_size),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

# Display progenies in numeric order; preserve the exported family_table object.
family_table[
  order(as.integer(sub("^PROG ", "", family_table$Progeny))),
  ,
  drop = FALSE
] |>
  knitr::kable(
    format = "html",
    row.names = FALSE,
    table.attr = 'class="table table-striped table-hover table-bordered" width="100%"',
    caption = "Number of genotyped individuals per progeny",
    col.names = c("Progeny", "Individuals")
  )

stopifnot(
  length(family_size) == 13L,
  all(family_size == 15L)
)
```

The table confirms the expected 13 groups of 15 plants. This balanced
representation describes the **observed target population**; it does not imply
that progeny labels are used to partition cross-validation folds.

### 5.2 Distribution of the three phenotypic targets

The genomic-prediction responses are the plant-level BLUPs of `Cer`
(cercosporiosis), `BM` (leaf-miner incidence), and `LP` (the
production-related trait) estimated in R01. Unlike the original annual
observations, each BLUP column contains one adjusted value per individual.
All three traits are summarized for the same 195 aligned plants.

The table reports the number of available and missing targets, the mean,
standard deviation, median, and range for each trait. These are descriptive
summaries of the saved BLUPs, not new mixed-model estimates.

```{r trait-summary}
traits <- c(
  "Cer",
  "BM",
  "LP"
)

trait_summary <- data.frame(
  Trait = character(0),
  N = integer(0),
  Missing = integer(0),
  Mean = numeric(0),
  SD = numeric(0),
  Min = numeric(0),
  Median = numeric(0),
  Max = numeric(0),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

for (trait in traits) {
  x <- blups[[trait]]

  trait_summary <- rbind(
    trait_summary,
    data.frame(
      Trait = trait,
      N = sum(!is.na(x)),
      Missing = sum(is.na(x)),
      Mean = mean(x, na.rm = TRUE),
      SD = sd(x, na.rm = TRUE),
      Min = min(x, na.rm = TRUE),
      Median = median(x, na.rm = TRUE),
      Max = max(x, na.rm = TRUE),
      stringsAsFactors = FALSE
    )
  )
}

trait_summary |>
  knitr::kable(
    format = "html",
    row.names = FALSE,
    table.attr = 'class="table table-striped table-hover table-bordered" width="100%"',
    digits = 4,
    caption = "Summary of individual BLUPs used as prediction targets",
    col.names = c(
      "Trait", "N", "Missing", "Mean", "SD", "Minimum", "Median", "Maximum"
    )
  )

stopifnot(
  all(traits %in% names(blups)),
  all(trait_summary$N == 195L),
  all(trait_summary$Missing == 0L)
)
```

The means and standard deviations should be interpreted within each trait:
`Cer` and `BM` are recorded on different response distributions from
`LP`. Differences in raw BLUP magnitude across traits therefore do not
represent differences in predictive performance. The following boxplots show
the median, interquartile range, and potential outlying values within each
trait. Independent vertical scales prevent the larger numerical range of
`LP` from hiding the variation in `Cer` and `BM`.

```{r blup-target-boxplots, fig.width=9, fig.height=5, fig.cap="Distribution of the saved plant-level BLUP targets for Cer, BM, and LP. Each panel uses its own vertical scale.", fig.alt="Three boxplots showing distributions of individual Cer, BM, and LP BLUPs, each with an independent vertical axis."}
# Reshape only a plotting copy; the 195-row BLUP table is not modified.
blup_boxplot_data <- rbind(
  data.frame(Trait = "Cer", BLUP = blups$Cer),
  data.frame(Trait = "BM", BLUP = blups$BM),
  data.frame(Trait = "LP", BLUP = blups$LP)
)

blup_boxplot_data$Trait <- factor(
  blup_boxplot_data$Trait,
  levels = traits
)

p_blup_targets <- ggplot(
  blup_boxplot_data,
  aes(x = Trait, y = BLUP, fill = Trait)
) +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.55, show.legend = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(~ Trait, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_fill_gdocs(limits = c("BM", "Cer", "LP")) +
  labs(x = "Trait", y = "Individual BLUP") +
  theme_gdocs()

print(p_blup_targets)
```

The boxplots display the same saved values summarized in the table above.
They do not select individuals, modify any BLUP, or provide inputs to
marker filtering. The subsequent SNP quality-control analysis uses
genotypes only.

## 6. Genotype coding and completeness

### 6.1 SNP genotype coding and allele dosage

The Capture-Seq matrix retains the discrete genotype coding
`-1`, `0`, and `1`: the two outer states correspond to the two
homozygous classes, and the middle state identifies heterozygotes.
Section 3.2 illustrates these codes in the raw SNP records.

For allele-frequency calculations in Section 7, adding one converts the
stored values to allele dosages:

| Stored SNP code (`G`) | Dosage (`G + 1`) | Genotype class |
|:---:|:---:|:---|
| `-1` | `0` | Homozygote for the allele represented by dosage zero |
| `0` | `1` | Heterozygote |
| `1` | `2` | Homozygote for the allele represented by dosage two |

Table: Genotype coding and the corresponding allele-dosage transformation

The conversion `G + 1` is used to calculate allele frequencies and MAF;
it does **not** replace the original `-1/0/1` coding in the matrix supplied
to the prediction models. The coding alone does not identify which allele is
the reference or alternate allele.

### 6.2 Genotype matrix structure and completeness

The next table summarizes the aligned matrix `G`, including its number of
individuals and raw SNPs, the observed genotype states, missing cells, and
duplicate identifiers. Checking these properties precedes marker filtering.
The original code then verifies that the three expected genotype states
are present and that individual and marker identifiers are unique.

```{r genotype-coding}
observed_codes <- sort(
  unique(
    as.numeric(G)
  )
)

genotype_summary <- data.frame(
  Statistic = c(
    "Individuals",
    "Raw SNPs",
    "Observed genotype codes",
    "Missing genotype cells",
    "Duplicated individual IDs",
    "Duplicated marker IDs"
  ),
  Value = c(
    as.character(nrow(G)),
    as.character(ncol(G)),
    paste(observed_codes, collapse = ", "),
    as.character(sum(is.na(G))),
    as.character(sum(duplicated(rownames(G)))),
    as.character(sum(duplicated(colnames(G))))
  ),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

genotype_summary |>
  knitr::kable(
    format = "html",
    row.names = FALSE,
    table.attr = 'class="table table-striped table-hover table-bordered" width="100%"',
    caption = "Structure of the Capture-Seq genotype matrix",
    col.names = c("Statistic", "Value")
  )

stopifnot(
  identical(
    observed_codes,
    c(-1, 0, 1)
  ),
  !anyDuplicated(rownames(G)),
  !anyDuplicated(colnames(G))
)
```

## 7. Marker quality control

### 7.1 Computing marker-level quality statistics

Marker quality control (QC) is applied to the 195 aligned genotype profiles
before the cross-validation partitions are created. The same retained SNPs
are subsequently supplied to every genomic-prediction method. SNP values
are not used to decide which individuals enter the validation folds.

Three criteria are evaluated separately for every marker:

1. **Call rate:** the proportion of individuals with a non-missing genotype.
   At least 90% of the 195 genotypes must be observed
   (`call_rate >= CALL_RATE_MIN`).
2. **Minor allele frequency (MAF):** the smaller of the two estimated
   allele frequencies. A marker is retained only when
   `maf >= MAF_MIN`, with `MAF_MIN = 0.05`.
3. **Observed heterozygosity:** the proportion of non-missing individuals
   coded as `0` (heterozygotes). Markers with all observed genotypes
   heterozygous have no genotype variation and are removed using
   `observed_heterozygosity < 1`.

For marker \(j\), the calculations correspond to

\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{CallRate}_j
  &= \frac{\text{number of observed genotypes at marker }j}{195},\\
p_j &= \frac{\operatorname{mean}(G_{ij}+1)}{2},\\
\mathrm{MAF}_j &= \min(p_j,1-p_j),\\
H_{O,j} &= \frac{\text{number of observed heterozygotes at marker }j}
{\text{number of observed genotypes at marker }j}.
\end{aligned}
\]

The allele-frequency and heterozygosity calculations exclude missing
genotypes (`na.rm = TRUE`). The additional `marker_variance` statistic
describes variation in the original `-1/0/1` coding; it is recorded for
inspection, **not used as a fourth marker-selection threshold**.

A SNP passes QC only if it meets **all three** criteria. The logical vector
`keep_marker` records this combined decision, while `marker_qc` retains
the statistics and individual pass/fail flags for all raw SNPs.

```{r marker-quality-control}
call_rate <- colMeans(
  !is.na(G)
)

dosage <- G + 1

allele_frequency <- colMeans(
  dosage,
  na.rm = TRUE
) / 2

maf <- pmin(
  allele_frequency,
  1 - allele_frequency
)

observed_heterozygosity <- colMeans(
  G == 0,
  na.rm = TRUE
)

marker_variance <- apply(
  G,
  2,
  var,
  na.rm = TRUE
)

pass_call_rate <- call_rate >= CALL_RATE_MIN
pass_maf <- maf >= MAF_MIN
pass_heterozygosity <- observed_heterozygosity < 1

keep_marker <- (
  pass_call_rate &
  pass_maf &
  pass_heterozygosity
)

marker_qc <- data.frame(
  Marker = colnames(G),
  Call_Rate = call_rate,
  Allele_Frequency = allele_frequency,
  MAF = maf,
  Observed_Heterozygosity = observed_heterozygosity,
  Variance = marker_variance,
  Pass_Call_Rate = pass_call_rate,
  Pass_MAF = pass_maf,
  Pass_Heterozygosity = pass_heterozygosity,
  Keep = keep_marker,
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

qc_summary <- data.frame(
  Criterion = c(
    "Raw SNPs",
    "Call rate < 0.90",
    "MAF < 0.05",
    "100% observed heterozygosity",
    "Total SNPs removed",
    "SNPs retained"
  ),
  Markers = c(
    ncol(G),
    sum(!pass_call_rate),
    sum(!pass_maf),
    sum(!pass_heterozygosity),
    sum(!keep_marker),
    sum(keep_marker)
  ),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

qc_summary |>
  knitr::kable(
    format = "html",
    row.names = FALSE,
    table.attr = 'class="table table-striped table-hover table-bordered" width="100%"',
    caption = "Marker quality-control summary",
    col.names = c("Criterion", "Markers")
  )
```

The table counts failures for each rule independently. `Total SNPs removed`
instead counts the **union** of failures, so a marker that fails two rules
is counted only once in that total. In the present dataset, there are
`r sum(!pass_call_rate)` markers below the call-rate threshold,
`r sum(!pass_maf)` below the MAF threshold, and
`r sum(!pass_heterozygosity)` with complete observed heterozygosity.
The `r sum(!keep_marker)` unique exclusions leave
`r format(sum(keep_marker), big.mark = ",")` SNPs from the
`r format(ncol(G), big.mark = ",")` raw Capture-Seq markers.

### 7.2 Examples of marker decisions

To connect the decision rules with actual SNP records, the next table
displays one low-MAF marker, one completely heterozygous marker, and
one retained marker. These are examples selected from `marker_qc`,
not an additional filter or a replacement for the complete QC table.
The `Keep` column identifies whether the SNP enters the common panel.

```{r marker-qc-examples}
# Select three illustrative SNP records without changing the QC results.
qc_example_rows <- c(
  which(!pass_maf)[1L],
  which(!pass_heterozygosity)[1L],
  which(keep_marker)[1L]
)

qc_examples <- marker_qc[
  qc_example_rows,
  c("Marker", "Call_Rate", "MAF", "Observed_Heterozygosity",
    "Variance", "Keep"),
  drop = FALSE
]

qc_examples <- cbind(
  Example = c("Below MAF threshold", "Fully heterozygous", "Retained"),
  qc_examples
)
rownames(qc_examples) <- NULL

qc_examples |>
  knitr::kable(
    format = "html",
    row.names = FALSE,
    table.attr = 'class="table table-striped table-hover table-bordered" width="100%"',
    digits = 4,
    caption = "Examples of excluded and retained Capture-Seq markers"
  )
```

### 7.3 Minor allele frequency distribution

The density plot shows the **raw** MAF distribution before filtering.
The dashed line marks `MAF_MIN = 0.05`; markers to its left fail the MAF
criterion. Markers can also fail the heterozygosity criterion when their
MAF is high (for example, a locus that is heterozygous in every plant).
The MAF curve therefore illustrates only one of the three QC rules
and does not independently describe the final retained panel.

```{r maf-distribution, fig.width=9, fig.height=5, fig.alt="Density of minor allele frequencies among raw Capture-Seq SNPs, with a dashed vertical line marking the 0.05 minimum MAF threshold.", fig.cap="Minor allele frequency distribution across the raw Capture-Seq SNP panel. The dashed line indicates the MAF threshold used for marker retention."}
maf_plot_data <- data.frame(
  MAF = maf,
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

p_maf <- ggplot(
  maf_plot_data,
  aes(
    x = MAF
  )
) +
  geom_density(
    alpha = 0.28,
    linewidth = 0.9
  ) +
  geom_vline(
    xintercept = MAF_MIN,
    linetype = "dashed",
    linewidth = 0.7
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Minor allele frequency",
    y = "Density"
  ) +
  theme_gdocs()

print(p_maf)
```

The original high-resolution TIFF export is retained below for
reproducibility, but is not evaluated or displayed during HTML rendering.
Consequently, the existing figure is not rewritten by a tutorial build.

```{r save-maf-tiff, eval=FALSE, include=FALSE}
dir.create(
  "output/real/audit/figures",
  showWarnings = FALSE,
  recursive = TRUE
)

ggsave(
  "output/real/audit/figures/marker_maf_distribution.tiff",
  plot = p_maf,
  device = "tiff",
  width = 8,
  height = 5,
  units = "in",
  dpi = 300,
  compression = "lzw"
)
```

## 8. Common marker panel

### 8.1 Constructing the retained SNP matrix

The three pass/fail conditions from Section 7 are combined into the logical
vector `keep_marker`. Selecting `G[, keep_marker, drop = FALSE]` creates
`G_qc`, the common genomic matrix used by R03 and the prediction modules.
The operation removes failing SNP **columns**, not individual plant rows.
It also preserves the original order and `-1/0/1` values of the retained
SNPs; neither missing-value imputation nor genotype recoding is performed
here.

The accompanying vectors of call rate, MAF, heterozygosity, and variance
are restricted to the same retained SNP columns. Their minima and maxima
summarize the panel after QC, while `marker_qc` continues to describe the
**complete original panel**. The display-only formatting below does not
modify the numerical values saved for later analyses.

```{r common-marker-panel}
G_qc <- G[
  ,
  keep_marker,
  drop = FALSE
]

retained_call_rate <- call_rate[
  keep_marker
]

retained_maf <- maf[
  keep_marker
]

retained_heterozygosity <- observed_heterozygosity[
  keep_marker
]

retained_variance <- marker_variance[
  keep_marker
]

marker_contract <- data.frame(
  Property = c(
    "Individuals",
    "Retained SNPs",
    "Minimum call rate",
    "Minimum MAF",
    "Maximum observed heterozygosity",
    "Minimum marker variance"
  ),
  Value = c(
    nrow(G_qc),
    ncol(G_qc),
    min(retained_call_rate),
    min(retained_maf),
    max(retained_heterozygosity),
    min(retained_variance)
  ),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

# Display counts as integers and frequencies as decimals; keep numeric source intact.
marker_contract_display <- marker_contract
marker_contract_display$Value <- c(
  format(
    marker_contract$Value[1:2],
    big.mark = ",", trim = TRUE, scientific = FALSE
  ),
  sprintf("%.4f", marker_contract$Value[-(1:2)])
)

marker_contract_display |>
  knitr::kable(
    format = "html",
    row.names = FALSE,
    table.attr = 'class="table table-striped table-hover table-bordered" width="100%"',
    caption = "Common genomic marker panel after quality control",
    col.names = c("Property", "Value")
  )

stopifnot(
  nrow(G_qc) == 195L,
  all(retained_call_rate >= CALL_RATE_MIN),
  all(retained_maf >= MAF_MIN),
  all(retained_heterozygosity < 1),
  all(retained_variance > 0),
  !anyDuplicated(colnames(G_qc))
)
```

The final genomic matrix therefore contains `r nrow(G_qc)` individuals and
`r format(ncol(G_qc), big.mark = ",")` SNPs. The `-1/0/1` genotype coding and
the SNP column order are preserved.

### 8.2 Inspecting the retained marker order

The following table selects the first six SNPs in `G_qc` and displays their
original QC statistics. Marker names come directly from the retained matrix,
while their properties are retrieved from `marker_qc`. This allows the
retained panel to be inspected without recreating or reordering the SNPs.

```{r retained-marker-example}
# Read the original QC properties for the first retained SNP columns.
retained_marker_example <- marker_qc[
  match(head(colnames(G_qc), 6L), marker_qc$Marker),
  c("Marker", "Call_Rate", "MAF", "Observed_Heterozygosity",
    "Variance"),
  drop = FALSE
]
rownames(retained_marker_example) <- NULL

retained_marker_example |>
  knitr::kable(
    format = "html",
    row.names = FALSE,
    table.attr = 'class="table table-striped table-hover table-bordered" width="100%"',
    digits = 4,
    caption = "First six SNPs in the common marker panel"
  )
```

The resulting `G_qc` matrix is included unchanged in the shared object
assembled in Section 9. The phenotype targets and individual order were
already fixed in Section 4; marker QC does not change their correspondence.
In R03, validation partitions are assigned to these same 195 individuals,
using the common panel defined here.

## 9. Shared object for genomic prediction

### 9.1 Assembling the shared data object

The preceding sections match each plant-level BLUP with its Capture-Seq profile
and select the shared SNP panel using fixed quality-control rules. The R02
result is assembled as `real_common`, a list that retains the individual and
marker order for pre-validation and genomic prediction.

| Element | Contents and role |
|---|---|
| `genotype` | `G_qc`, with 195 plant rows and the retained SNP columns, in the original `-1/0/1` coding |
| `phenotype` | `Phenotype_ID` and the saved `Cer`, `BM`, and `LP` plant-level BLUPs, ordered to match the genomic rows |
| `individuals` | Mapping among `Phenotype_ID`, `Genotype_ID`, `ID_Planta`, `Progenie`, `Planta`, and `Populacao` |
| `traits` | Names of the three prediction responses |
| `family` | Progeny labels, named by `Phenotype_ID`, for the same 195 plants |
| `marker_qc` | QC statistics and retention decisions for every marker in the **raw** Capture-Seq panel |
| `metadata` | Source information, panel dimensions, genotype coding and fixed QC settings |

Table: Contents of the shared R02 object used in subsequent analyses

The `genotype` matrix contains only **retained** SNPs; `marker_qc` still
documents the original panel, including excluded loci. The rows of `genotype`
and `phenotype` refer to the same plants, in the same order. The chunk below
assembles the shared object without fitting prediction models or altering the
original marker-selection rules.

```{r build-common-object}
phenotype_targets <- blups[
  ,
  c(
    "Phenotype_ID",
    "Cer",
    "BM",
    "LP"
  )
]

real_common <- list(
  genotype = G_qc,
  phenotype = phenotype_targets,
  individuals = individuals,
  traits = traits,
  family = setNames(
    family,
    individuals$Phenotype_ID
  ),
  marker_qc = marker_qc,
  metadata = list(
    dataset = "real",
    species = "Coffea arabica",
    genotyping_method = "Capture-Seq",
    individuals = nrow(G_qc),
    raw_markers = ncol(G),
    retained_markers = ncol(G_qc),
    genotype_coding = c(-1, 0, 1),
    dosage_conversion = "G + 1",
    call_rate_threshold = CALL_RATE_MIN,
    maf_threshold = MAF_MIN,
    heterozygosity_rule = "observed heterozygosity < 1",
    progenies = length(unique(family))
  )
)
```

### 9.2 Saved outputs and their uses

The original preprocessing stage produced one shared RDS object and five
companion CSV files. The RDS retains the original R structures, whereas the
CSV files permit inspection of the SNP filtering, the BLUP summaries, and
individual identification. The additional TIFF is the high-resolution
version of the MAF figure from Section 7.

| Output file (relative to `output/real/audit/`) | Contents and intended use |
|---|---|
| `preprocessed_real_common.rds` | Complete `real_common` list; primary input to R03 |
| `real_marker_qc.csv` | Per-marker allele frequency, MAF, call rate, heterozygosity, variance, and QC decisions |
| `real_qc_summary.csv` | Counts of the original, excluded, and retained SNPs |
| `real_trait_summary.csv` | Descriptive summaries of the three saved phenotypic BLUP targets |
| `real_family_structure.csv` | Number of individuals in each progeny |
| `real_individual_map.csv` | Mapping among phenotypic, genomic, and field identifiers |
| `figures/marker_maf_distribution.tiff` | High-resolution MAF distribution figure |

Table: Saved real-data preprocessing outputs and their downstream roles

The pre-validation module R03 (`real_data_validation.Rmd`) reads
`preprocessed_real_common.rds` and uses `common$genotype`,
`common$phenotype`, and `common$traits`. It checks the alignment of 195
individuals and the 20,887-marker panel before assigning cross-validation
folds. The additional elements remain available for auditing and reuse.

The export code below preserves the original scientific file names, object
contents, and file-writing operations. It remains in the RMarkdown for
reproducibility but is disabled during site rendering
(`eval=FALSE, include=FALSE`). Thus, HTML generation does not overwrite the
persisted RDS or CSV outputs.

```{r save-common-outputs, eval=FALSE, include=FALSE}
saveRDS(
  real_common,
  "output/real/audit/preprocessed_real_common.rds",
  compress = "gzip"
)

write.csv(
  marker_qc,
  "output/real/audit/real_marker_qc.csv",
  row.names = FALSE
)

write.csv(
  qc_summary,
  "output/real/audit/real_qc_summary.csv",
  row.names = FALSE
)

write.csv(
  trait_summary,
  "output/real/audit/real_trait_summary.csv",
  row.names = FALSE
)

write.csv(
  family_table,
  "output/real/audit/real_family_structure.csv",
  row.names = FALSE
)

write.csv(
  individuals,
  "output/real/audit/real_individual_map.csv",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

## 10. Prepared input for the next modules

The real-data preprocessing establishes a single, aligned genomic-prediction
input for the subsequent modules:

- **Individuals:** 195 target plants from 13 experimental progenies, each
  represented by one matched genotype profile and one set of phenotypic BLUPs.
- **Prediction targets:** the previously estimated `Cer`, `BM`, and `LP`
  BLUPs from R01, in the same individual order as the genomic matrix.
- **Genomic markers:** `r format(ncol(G_qc), big.mark = ",")` retained SNPs
  from `r format(ncol(G), big.mark = ",")` raw Capture-Seq loci.
- **Genotype representation:** original `-1/0/1` codes, with retained
  marker names and column order preserved.
- **Reusable output:** `real_common` contains the common genotype and
  phenotype inputs, individual correspondence, progeny membership,
  marker-level QC information and preprocessing settings.

The next stage, **R03 — Pre-validation**, reads the saved RDS object and
constructs repeated nested cross-validation partitions from the aligned
individual IDs. The partitioning step does not repeat the SNP filters or
the genotype–phenotype matching. Its outputs are used by the GBLUP and
regularized ANN model-fitting modules.

R02 does not estimate genomic-prediction models or assess their performance;
it establishes the data and quality-control decisions shared by those models.
